overview.text: Major depressive disorder is a persistent depressive state with loss of interest or pleasure plus associated symptoms that impair function, typically without any history of mania or hypomania. Diagnosis is clinical under ICD-11 and DSM-5-TR, and remains a disorder of description rather than of any single laboratory test.

The large ENIGMA imaging studies show real but small average brain differences, with the most robust finding being slightly smaller hippocampi in recurrent and adult-onset illness. These group effects are too small to diagnose an individual, and their main value is mechanistic.

Antidepressant response rates are modest and roughly half of patients do not remit on the first adequate trial, so guidelines emphasise combined pharmacological and psychological treatment, measurement-based care, and early review of partial response. Suicide risk requires direct assessment at every contact.

description.text: Pervasively low or irritable mood most of the day, nearly every day. It is the core symptom of the episode and lifts with treatment in the majority of patients.

Loss of pleasure and diminished interest in previously rewarding activity, which drives the low drive and social withdrawal of depression. Reward-learning circuitry is central to how this domain is modelled.

Rumination, worry and physical anxiety symptoms are extremely common in depression and often persist after mood improves. Treating them explicitly improves outcome and is required when they cross the threshold for a separate anxiety disorder.
Persistent physical or mental tiredness that is not proportionate to activity and does not resolve with rest. It is one of the most disabling symptoms and often the last to remit.

Slower processing speed, impaired attention and executive function, and reduced working memory, which persist in a substantial minority even after mood remission and are a major obstacle to returning to work.

Insomnia or hypersomnia, and either loss of appetite with weight loss or increased appetite with weight gain. The pattern tracks with the more activated versus more melancholic presentation and predicts response to some drug classes.

Hopelessness, guilt and suicidal thinking, which carry most of the mortality of depression. Risk is highest in young men early in the illness and in people recently hospitalised, so direct enquiry at every contact is essential and a protective plan is part of care.

claim.text: In 1728 patients and 7199 controls the ENIGMA working group found significantly smaller hippocampi in depression, about one percent smaller in volume, and a larger effect in recurrent than single-episode illness.
The same study detected no difference between first-episode patients and controls, so the hippocampal finding reflects illness burden rather than the presence of depression at first presentation.

Patients whose illness began at or before age 21 showed a trend toward smaller amygdalae alongside the hippocampal effect. The source reports the whole amygdala, so it is applied across all four amygdala sub-meshes here and flagged as a proxy.

In the same early-onset subgroup the lateral ventricles were about five percent larger, one of the larger relative differences reported. This is a group finding and is not a diagnostic marker for an individual patient.

claim.text: Across 2148 patients and 7957 controls from 20 sites, adults with depression had thinner cortex in orbitofrontal, anterior and posterior cingulate, insular and temporal regions, with effect sizes between minus 0.10 and minus 0.14. The atlas has no single orbitofrontal or cingulate mesh, so documented gyral proxies are used and flagged.

Adolescents with depression had lower total cortical surface area but no thickness difference, with regional reductions in medial orbitofrontal and superior frontal cortex and in visual, somatosensory and motor areas, with effect sizes between minus 0.26 and minus 0.57. The effect size shown here is the midpoint of that reported range and is not a single study estimate.

Diffusion imaging in 1305 patients and 1602 controls found subtly lower fractional anisotropy in 16 of 25 tracts examined, with effect sizes between 0.12 and 0.26 and the largest differences in the corpus callosum and corona radiata. The effect size shown here is the midpoint of that range.

function.text: Blunted responsiveness to reward in ventral striatum and hippocampus underlies anhedonia and the reduced motivation of depression. This circuit is the target of behavioural activation and of antidepressants that gradually restore reward learning.

function.text: Weakened prefrontal control of attention and rumination explains the cognitive and worry symptoms of depression. Genetic enrichment in prefrontal regions across depression GWAS points to the same location.

atlasLabels: Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Middle anterior part)

edges.to: Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Middle anterior part)

function.text: Amygdala, hippocampus and anterior cingulate work together to appraise threat and generate mood. Disrupted interaction in this loop underlies the anxiety, guilt and low mood of depression, and each node is a documented site of the cortical thinning found in adults.

Stress-system activation links sleep, appetite and mood disturbance in depression. The adrenal cortex that completes this axis has no mesh in the atlas, so the loop is drawn only as far as the hypothalamic and brainstem structures that are resolved, with the locus coeruleus as a schematic marker.

neurochemistry.alteration: Reduced serotonergic function, the target of most first-line antidepressants

claim.text: Serotonin reuptake inhibition is the shared mechanism of most antidepressants used in depression, though benefit appears to depend on downstream plasticity rather than on correcting a simple serotonin deficit.

neurochemistry.alteration: Reduced noradrenergic drive contributing to fatigue and poor concentration

claim.text: Locus coeruleus noradrenergic projections to cortex and hippocampus are the basis for the noradrenergic antidepressants and for the attention and energy symptoms of depression. The locus coeruleus itself is not resolved by the atlas and is shown as a calibrated marker.

Blunted striatal reward responsiveness underlies anhedonia, which is why noradrenergic-dopaminergic antidepressants such as bupropion are effective and why activation of reward learning is a behavioural treatment target.

neurochemistry.alteration: Glutamatergic system impairment, the target of the newest rapid-acting antidepressants

claim.text: NMDA receptor antagonism with esketamine produces rapid antidepressant effects through downstream AMPA signalling, and synaptic and neurotransmitter gene sets are among those enriched in large genetic studies of depression.
Reduced neurotrophic support for synaptic remodelling in hippocampus and prefrontal cortex is the neuroplasticity account of depression, consistent with BDNF-pathway enrichment in depression GWAS.

architecture.text: A meta-analysis of three genome-wide studies covering 807553 people identified 102 independent variants, 269 genes and 15 gene sets associated with depression, and 87 of the 102 variants replicated in a further 1306354 individuals.

The associated genes and gene sets were enriched for synaptic structure and neurotransmission, and enrichment analysis specifically implicated prefrontal brain regions, matching the cortical imaging findings.

Because no single variant accounts for more than a small share of liability, depression is taught as a polygenic disorder in which environment, illness burden and treatment response all matter. Candidate-gene findings such as the serotonin transporter promoter polymorphism are real but small and debated, so no large effect is claimed for them.

finding.text: Smaller hippocampi are the most replicated structural finding in depression, with a standardised difference around 0.14 that is absent in first-episode illness. The group difference is far too small to distinguish an individual patient from a control.

Diffusion imaging shows subtle widespread anisotropy reductions in adult depression, driven by recurrent and adult-onset illness. It is a research marker with no established clinical interpretation for an individual.

Peripheral inflammatory markers are modestly elevated on average in depression and in psychosis risk, but heterogeneity is high and no threshold has diagnostic value. Inflammation is best treated as a group-level research signal, not a clinical test.

The combination of orbitofrontal, cingulate, insular and temporal thinning in adults with lower surface area in adolescents is reasonably reproducible, and enrichment analysis also points to prefrontal regions genetically. It remains a research pattern rather than a diagnostic one.

pathway.step: Mild to moderate: drug or psychotherapy, either first

claim.text: For mild to moderate depression, guidelines support offering either an antidepressant or structured psychotherapy as a first option, since both work and some patients prefer to avoid medication initially. Choice should follow patient preference, prior response and comorbidity.

pathway.step: Moderate to severe or prior response: combine

claim.text: For more severe illness or a previous good response, guidelines recommend combined pharmacological and psychological treatment, choosing a drug class by symptom pattern such as insomnia or weight concern rather than by a single protocol for everyone.

pathway.step: Partial response: measure and switch or augment

claim.text: After an adequate trial with partial improvement, guidelines advise measuring symptom change objectively, then switching class or augmenting. Optimising the dose and duration comes before any switch, and a second adequate trial should use a different mechanism.

pathway.step: Treatment resistance or urgent need: rapid and somatic options

claim.text: Treatment resistance, or urgent need such as severe suicidality or catatonia, leads to electroconvulsive therapy, ketamine or esketamine, and neuromodulation. Vagus nerve stimulation is reserved for the most refractory cases and its evidence is mixed: the RECOVER trial missed its prespecified primary endpoint while several secondary measures favoured active stimulation.

After remission, continuing antidepressant medication for at least six to twelve months and adding relapse-prevention strategies such as mindfulness-based cognitive therapy reduces recurrence. Medication should be tapered slowly and not stopped abruptly.

tour.title: 1 · A polygenic illness with a prefrontal signature
tour.text: Over 800000 people in one analysis yielded 102 independent variants, with the associated genes pointing at synaptic transmission and at prefrontal cortex. No single gene causes depression.

tour.title: 2 · The hippocampus is consistently smaller
tour.text: Across 1728 patients the ENIGMA group found smaller hippocampi, a standardised difference near 0.14 that appears only with recurrent or adult-onset illness and is absent at first episode.

tour.title: 3 · Prefrontal and limbic cortex thin
tour.text: Adults show thinning in orbitofrontal, cingulate, insular and temporal cortex with small effects. Adolescents show reduced surface area instead, in frontal and sensory areas with much larger effects.

tour.title: 4 · White matter loses integrity
tour.text: Sixteen of twenty-five tracts showed lower fractional anisotropy, largest in the corpus callosum and corona radiata, suggesting distributed disconnectivity rather than one damaged tract.

tour.title: 5 · Reward circuitry explains anhedonia
tour.text: Ventral striatum, hippocampus and parahippocampal input form the reward circuit whose blunted responsiveness produces anhedonia and low drive.

tour.title: 6 · Serotonin, noradrenaline, glutamate
tour.text: Raphe and locus coeruleus drive feed cortex and limbic structures; the newest rapid-acting drugs work on glutamate instead. Both brainstem nuclei are shown as schematic markers because the atlas does not resolve them.

tour.title: 7 · Treatment is stepped, and resistance is real
tour.text: Drug or therapy first, combine for moderate illness, switch class on partial response, and use ECT or ketamine when urgent, with neuromodulation for the most refractory cases.

quiz.question: Which ICD-11 codes cover single-episode and recurrent depressive disorder?
choices: 6A70 and 6A71
6A20 and 6A21
6B00 and 6B01
6A60 and 6A61
quiz.explanation: ICD-11 uses 6A70 for single episode depressive disorder and 6A71 for recurrent depressive disorder, both inside the mood and affective disorders block.

quiz.question: Which symptom pair is core to a depressive episode?
choices: Auditory hallucinations and delusions
Low mood and loss of pleasure
Elevated mood and reduced need for sleep
Obsessions and compulsions
quiz.explanation: Depressed mood and anhedonia are the two core symptoms; the other pairs belong to psychosis, mania and obsessive-compulsive disorder.

quiz.question: A patient's anhedonia and fatigue resolve fully once sleep and an antidepressant are corrected. What does this suggest?
choices: The original episode was severe
Some symptoms were secondary to sleep disturbance or medication
The diagnosis was incorrect
Insight is impaired
quiz.explanation: Sleep, appetite and fatigue symptoms are frequently secondary and reversible, which is why guidelines emphasise treating them directly rather than assuming they all reflect core illness.

quiz.question: What did the ENIGMA subcortical study find in depression, and for whom?
choices: Larger hippocampi, strongest in first episode
Smaller hippocampi, stronger in recurrent and early-onset illness
No differences in any subgroup
Larger amygdalae only
quiz.explanation: Hippocampal volume was about one percent smaller overall, with a larger effect in recurrent depression and no difference at first episode, plus smaller amygdalae and larger ventricles in the early-onset subgroup.

quiz.question: How did cortical findings differ between adults and adolescents with depression?
choices: Adults thinner, adolescents lower surface area without thickness change
Both showed the same pattern
Adults had larger surface area, adolescents thicker cortex
No differences in either group
quiz.explanation: Adults showed thinning in orbitofrontal, cingulate, insular and temporal cortex with small effects, while adolescents had lower total surface area and much larger regional effects without a thickness difference.

quiz.question: What did the ENIGMA diffusion study report?
choices: Lower fractional anisotropy in 16 of 25 tracts, largest in corpus callosum and corona radiata
Higher anisotropy throughout
Differences only in children
No white-matter differences
quiz.explanation: Subtle widespread anisotropy reductions with standardised differences of 0.12 to 0.26, driven by recurrent adult-onset illness, suggest distributed disconnectivity.

quiz.question: What did the large PGC depression meta-analysis identify?
choices: A single causal gene
102 independent variants, 269 genes and 15 gene sets, enriched for synaptic function
No heritable component
Only rare recessive variants
quiz.explanation: Analysing 807553 individuals yielded 102 independent variants, with synaptic structure and neurotransmission gene sets enriched and prefrontal regions highlighted, 87 of 102 variants replicating independently.

quiz.question: What is the shared molecular mechanism of most first-line antidepressants?
choices: Dopamine D2 blockade
Serotonin transporter inhibition
Muscarinic agonism
NMDA receptor activation
quiz.explanation: SSRIs and related agents block the serotonin transporter, though benefit appears to require downstream plasticity rather than a simple correction of serotonin deficiency.

quiz.question: Which brainstem nucleus is shown as a schematic marker rather than a mesh, and why does it matter?
choices: Substantia nigra, because it is too small
Locus coeruleus, because the atlas cannot resolve it though it is central to noradrenergic antidepressants
Hippocampus, because it is not a nucleus
Amygdala, because it is four separate meshes
quiz.explanation: The locus coeruleus is the source of cortical noradrenaline and the target of noradrenergic drug classes, but the atlas has no mesh for it, so it is shown as a calibrated marker labelled schematic.

quiz.question: How do ketamine and esketamine differ from monoamine antidepressants in speed of action?
choices: They act within hours through NMDA antagonism and downstream AMPA signalling
They act only after several weeks
They act faster because they block dopamine
They work by enhancing serotonin release
quiz.explanation: NMDA antagonism triggers a glutamate surge and plasticity signalling, which explains their rapid antidepressant effect and why they are given in a monitored setting.

quiz.question: Which adverse effect cluster is characteristic of tricyclics like amitriptyline, and which receptors produce it?
choices: Weight gain and sedation from D2 blockade
Anticholinergic, orthostatic and sedating effects from muscarinic, alpha-1 and histamine blockade
Akathisia from partial agonism
Hyperprolactinaemia from dopamine blockade
quiz.explanation: Tricyclics combine serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibition with muscarinic, alpha-1 and histamine antagonism, which produces dry mouth, constipation, orthostasis, sedation and cardiotoxic overdose risk.

quiz.question: A depressed patient has insomnia and poor appetite. Which drug class is often preferred, and at what cost?
choices: An SSRI, at the cost of insomnia
Mirtazapine, because of alpha-2A and H1 blockade, at the cost of weight gain and sedation
Bupropion, because of dopamine blockade, at the cost of akathisia
Haloperidol, at the cost of tremor
quiz.explanation: Mirtazapine blocks alpha-2A autoreceptors to raise monoamines while blocking H1 to improve sleep and appetite, with weight gain and residual sedation as the trade-off.

quiz.question: What does the RECOVER trial of vagus nerve stimulation in markedly treatment-resistant depression actually show?
choices: Clear superiority on the prespecified primary endpoint
The prespecified primary endpoint did not separate from sham, while several secondary symptom, function and quality-of-life measures favoured active stimulation
No effect on any measure at any timepoint
A significant reduction in completed suicide
quiz.explanation: This mixed result is reported honestly: the primary outcome did not differentiate the groups, but symptom, function and quality-of-life secondary measures favoured active stimulation, and benefits were durable at 18 to 24 months.

quiz.question: Which neuromodulation has the strongest guideline support for treatment-resistant depression?
choices: Deep brain stimulation of the ventral striatum
Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex
Vagus nerve stimulation from implanted electrodes
Transcranial focused ultrasound
quiz.explanation: rTMS over left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex is guideline-supported for treatment-resistant depression, while implanted VNS and other surgical options are reserved for the most refractory cases with weaker evidence.

quiz.question: How should hippocampal volume be used in depression?
choices: To diagnose depression in an individual patient
As a mechanistic research finding, since the group difference is too small for individuals
To choose between SSRIs and tricyclics
To predict antidepressant response reliably
quiz.explanation: The hippocampal effect is real and replicated but averages around 0.14 standardised difference, and it is absent in first-episode illness, so it informs mechanism rather than individual diagnosis or treatment choice.

quiz.question: For mild to moderate depression, what do guidelines say about starting choice?
choices: Medication is always required
Either an antidepressant or structured psychotherapy may be offered first, guided by patient preference
Electroconvulsive therapy is first line
Polypharmacy is recommended
quiz.explanation: Both medication and structured psychotherapy are first-line options for mild to moderate depression, and preference and prior response should drive the choice rather than a single mandated protocol.
